picks.title: EPISODE 3: For Heaven's Sake
picks.summary: In Episode 3, Shofar, So Good! host Kate Mishkin delves into havruta learning, the Jewish tradition of studying Torah in pairs. The goal of this paired endeavor: arguing "for the sake of heaven." Kate explores what exactly that means, teaches us about Jewish history's most famous study partners, and learns how AI is changing havruta learning. Then, Kate and her dad become havrutas. Further reading and resources: •  Havruta: Learning in Pairs (My Jewish Learning) • Project Zug •  Whole and Broken Tablets: Aging in Rabbinic Literature (Project Zug) •  Beit Midrash Research Project (Brandeis Univ
picks.reason: Explores Jewish havruta study and its ethical ideal of arguing for heaven's sake.

picks.title: Michelle Farber: Bringing Talmud to the World
picks.summary:
The Talmud is the foundational text of Judaism — every law, every debate, every dissenting opinion preserved across 2,711 pages. For centuries it was accessible only to scholars. That is changing.
Rabbanit Michelle Farber is the founder of Hadran and the host of Daf Yomi for Women, the first and only women's daily Daf Yomi podcast. From her dining room table in Israel, she has built a worldwide movement — bringing daily Talmud study into the lives of thousands of women and men from all backgrounds.
The story of how the Talmud went from the study halls of the few to the daily lives of the many
picks.reason: Discusses making Talmud study accessible and its spiritual significance.

picks.title: R. Avital Hochstein on Parashat Ki Tavo: Clearing the Holy from the Home
picks.summary: Our parashah describes a ceremony known as vidui ma’aser.  The word vidui here from the root י.ד.ה. probably means something like “declaration of thanks” (like the prayer Modim), but can be also literally translated as “confession,” like the vidui familiar to us from our High Holiday liturgy.  What at first seems like an idyllic description of a perfect covenant in our land turns, through a reading of a Medieval commentator, into a pathway to move forward after sin and covenantal rupture.
picks.reason: Explores a Torah portion's ceremony as a path after sin and covenant rupture.

picks.title: An Eye for an Eye - What It Actually Meant, From Babylon to Yeshua
picks.summary: Diane kicks off a series on difficult biblical passages by reexamining the often-misquoted “an eye for an eye,” arguing it’s commonly treated as “vibes” instead of read in context. picks.reason: A serious, contextual study of Torah law on justice and punishment, tracing biblical and historical roots.

Home isn't a place with walls, it's the whole earth, and teshuva means returning to that sense of belonging. Josh also includes a short breath and gravity mindfulness practice to embody the idea.

picks.title: Read it both ways  - Rabbi Candice Levy
picks.summary: Ki Tavo offers a theology of reward and punishment, of cause and effect, but lived experience teaches us that the world does not work so neatly. What becomes possible when we read the parashah forwards and backwards, not only as protest against injustice, but also as a guide to rebuilding a shattered world?
picks.reason: A nuanced reading of parashah Ki Tavo on justice and rebuilding, engaging Jewish theology.

picks.title: Chullin 126 - Like a Rolling Stone
picks.summary:
On today’s page, Chullin 126, the rabbis encounter a mystery buried in two words: golel and dofek. Solving it takes us from Rashi and Maimonides to the burial caves of ancient Israel and the great stones once rolled across their entrances. What can the Talmud teach us about the lost burial practices of our ancestors? Listen and find out.

picks.reason: Talmudic study revealing ancient Jewish burial customs and their ethical implications.
